nodes.name: Creosote bush
nodes.desc: A common evergreen desert shrub of the Chihuahuan Desert flats. Its flowers feed bees, and GloBI records show honey bees and other insects using it.

nodes.name: Lechuguilla
nodes.desc: An indicator plant of the Chihuahuan Desert that spreads by underground offshoots into large colonies. Collared peccaries eat much of it in some areas.

nodes.name: Prickly pear
nodes.desc: One of the many cacti of Big Bend. Peccaries rely on prickly pear, and honey bees visit its flowers.

nodes.name: Desert grasses
nodes.desc: Grama grasses of the grasslands on the park's igneous and limestone soils and along the river. Their seeds and leaves feed rodents, doves, rabbits and deer.

nodes.name: Western honey bee
nodes.desc: Collects nectar and pollen from desert flowers such as creosote and prickly pear. Roadrunners and bears also eat honey bees in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Merriam's kangaroo rat
nodes.desc: Eats mostly seeds and stores them in its burrow. It rarely drinks, getting water from its food and its humid burrow.

nodes.name: Desert cottontail
nodes.desc: A rabbit of open desert scrub that grazes on grasses and other plants. Coyotes, foxes and rattlesnakes hunt it.

nodes.name: White-winged dove
nodes.desc: One of the most commonly recorded birds in the park area. It eats seeds and fruit and is taken by coyotes.

nodes.name: Collared peccary
nodes.desc: Also called javelina. Its main foods are agaves and prickly pears, and its predators include cougars and coyotes.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The park's main hoofed prey. Cougar hunting centres on deer, and coyotes eat them too. A small Chisos Mountains population is well known.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A clever omnivore that scavenges carcasses. It is one of the most frequently recorded birds in the park area.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Eats almost only carrion and finds it by smell. Recorded far more than any other species near the park, it cleans up dead animals.

nodes.name: Greater roadrunner
nodes.desc: A fast ground cuckoo that eats insects, spiders, mice, lizards and young rattlesnakes.

nodes.name: Western diamondback rattlesnake
nodes.desc: Ambush predator of rodents, rabbits and birds. Young snakes are eaten by roadrunners, and coyotes also take it.

nodes.name: Gray fox
nodes.desc: A small omnivorous canid seen near campsites at night. Eats rodents, rabbits and fruit.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: Lives in the Chisos Mountains. An omnivore that eats deer, small rodents and bee nests, and often steals cougar kills.

nodes.name: Cougar
nodes.desc: Roughly two dozen live in the park. Deer are its chief prey, with peccaries also taken. When big prey is scarce it eats smaller animals.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: The most widespread predator, with GloBI records of it eating deer, peccary, rabbits, rodents, birds and rattlesnakes.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong desert sun drives plant growth, but it also dries the land and heats it, so most animals are active at dawn, dusk or night.

nodes.name: Scarce rain
nodes.desc: Rainfall in the park ranges from about 10 inches a year at Castolon to 18 in the Chisos Basin. Plant growth depends on it.

nodes.name: Rio Grande & springs
nodes.desc: The river and desert springs create a green riparian strip and isolated wet habitats across the dry landscape.

nodes.name: Desert soil
nodes.desc: Thin soils of igneous and limestone origin. Nutrients return to them from dead plants and animals.

nodes.name: Soil microbes & fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.
